HEARD:
December 21, 2010

the honourable mr. justice p.b. hambly

reasons
for judgment

[
1
]

This is an appeal by the father from an order
obtained by summary judgment granting the CAS Crown Wardship with no access to
his three children.

The Facts

Procedural History

[
2
]

J.R. (“J.R.”) and K.M. (“K.M.”) are the parents
of the following children:

K.
born July […], 2002 – age 8

D.1
born October […], 2005 – age 5

D.2 born February […], 2008 – age 2

The CAS apprehended the children on September 30, 2009.  They placed
them with T.G. (“T.G.”) and P.G..  T.G. is the mother of K.M..  J.R. retained
Mr. P. Brohman and K.M. retained Mr. D. Lang.  The CAS issued a protection application
first returnable on October 5, 2009 in which it sought a supervision order for
eight months with the children being placed with T.G..  A settlement conference
took place on February 19, 2009.  Mr. J.R. would not consent to the order
sought by the CAS.  On March 24, 2010 the case came before Justice Hardman.
With the consent of J.R., Mr. Brohman was removed from the record as his
lawyer.  J.R. gave his address as R[…] East, Number 14, in Kitchener.  A trial
was set for June 7-11.  A trial management conference was set for May 18.

[
3
]

On April 27, 2010 K.M. and J.R. were arrested
for possession of marijuana for the purpose of trafficking.  J.R. was released
on bail on terms that he reside with his mother at 43A Manitoba Street in
Bracebridge.

[
4
]

The CAS sent a letter dated May 5, 2010 to the Kitchener
address that J.R. gave confirming the date of the trial management conference
on May 18, 2010.  On May 10, the CAS served J.R. by courier with its trial
management conference brief by leaving a copy at the Kitchener address.  It
stated that the Society would amend its protection application to seek Crown
Wardship without access.  J.R. did not attend the trial management conference. Maria
Stefan (“Maria”), who was the child protection worker in charge of the case,
left a message at his mother's home in Bracebridge on May 19, 2010 that the
case had been adjourned at the trial management conference the previous day to
June 2, 2010 for summary judgment.

[
5
]

On Thursday, May 27, 2010, Purolator Courier
picked up at the CAS office in Hespeler the notice of motion for summary
judgement returnable in Kitchener on Wednesday, June 2010 and the supporting
affidavit of Maria, for service on J.R. at 43A Manitoba Street in Bracebridge.
Both documents were dated May 27, 2010.  Purolator delivered these documents on
Friday, May 28, 2010 to J.R..

[
6
]

On May 28, 2010, the CAS amended the already
amended protection application to seek Crown Wardship without access.  On
Tuesday June 1, 2010, the CAS served J.R. personally in Bracebridge with the
amended amended application.  On the same day, Maria spoke to J.R. by
telephone.  He confirmed that he had received the documents of the CAS.  He
stated that he was trying to retain a lawyer in Cambridge.  He stated that he
was prevented from coming to Kitchener by the terms of his bail.  He stated further
"I was fighting you guys but not anymore, I was using a lot of drugs, I
was selfish, I did not think straight, I do not want to live like that anymore,
I do not want to go to trial, I want you guys to help me be a better father to
my kids".

[
7
]

On Wednesday, June 2, 2010, the matter came
before Justice M. McSorley.  Mr. Lang appeared.  Justice McSorley granted a
motion that Mr. Lang had brought removing him from the record.  J.R. did not
appear.  Justice McSorley granted the application of the CAS for Crown Wardship
with no access.  On Friday, June 4, 2010, Maria spoke with J.R..  She told him
the result.  He told her that he wanted to get his children back.

[
8
]

J.R. filed an affidavit sworn September 24, 2010
in which he concedes that he was served with the amended amended protection
application of the CAS seeking Crown Wardship and the notice of motion by which
the CAS sought summary judgment.  He stated that it was always his
understanding that the CAS was seeking to place the children with T.G..  He
stated the following:

...

8.    When I was served with the Summary Judgment
Motion materials and the Amended Amended Application, they looked to me like
duplicates of materials with which I had been previously served.  I had no idea
that I needed to respond.

9.    I did not have the assistance of a lawyer at
that time, did not read these materials properly, and thinking they were
duplicates, put them aside and did not provide them to my appeal counsel for
the preparation of the Notice of Appeal.

10.  All I know is that as soon as I heard that a
decision had been made in the court in my absence that the children are to be
made Crown Wards without me having any access, I was terribly shocked and
immediately took steps to appeal the decision.

11.  Firmly believing it to be true, I told my
appeal counsel that I had not been served with materials that gave me notice of
a change in the society’s position.

12.  I have a strong bond with my children and love
to be with them.

13.  I have engaged in programs to better myself as
a parent and a person.

14.  I wish to have an opportunity to prove my
ability to act as a proper parent to my children at a trial.

15.  I wish to respond with an Answer to the Amended
Amended Application served on me on June 1, 2010.

16.  I also wish to respond to the Summary Judgment
motion materials, should this Honourable Court uphold the validity of the
Summary Judgment motion per se and allow such a proceeding to be scheduled.

The Evidence

[
9
]

In the amended protection application dated
October 2, 2009 the CAS sought a finding under the
Child and Family Services
Act
that the children were in need of protection because of a risk that
they were likely to suffer physical and emotional harm caused by the failure of
K.M. and J.R. to provide adequate care to them and of a pattern of neglect
while they were in their care pursuant to sections 37(2)(b)(i) and (ii) of the
Act.  The CAS sought an order that the children be placed with T.G. for eight
months, subject to the supervision of the Society.  It sought an order that the
access of K.M. and J.R. to the children be supervised by the CAS and be at its
discretion.

[
10
]

J.R. filed an answer dated December 3, 2009 in
which he did not challenge the position of the CAS that the children were in
need of protection.  He denied most of the allegations made by the Society in
its application.  He did not provide particulars of his position on these
allegations.  He denied that the children were at risk in his care.  He sought
an order that the children be placed with him.  He provided no particulars as
to how he would care for them.  He stated only that he was "working on my
issues to be the best possible father of the children".

[
11
]

Maria has been a family service worker with the
CAS since May 2003.  She has been the family service worker for the M. family
since May 2009.  She filed an affidavit sworn October 2, 2009 and an affidavit
sworn May 27, 2010 in which she outlined the history of the involvement of the
CAS with the M. family.  The CAS has been involved with the M. family since
November 2002.  There have been many allegations of violence between J.R. and K.M..
At times, J.R. has been prohibited by a restraining order from communicating
with Tyler.  Both he and K.M. ignored the order.  Both K.M. and J.R. have
abused prescription and non-prescription drugs including Oxycontin, Percocet,
cocaine and marijuana.  They have both been on a methadone program with limited
success.  The parents have frequently been separated.  The children have
resided mainly with K.M..  She frequently resided with the children with her
mother, T.G., her father, T.M. and other relatives.  She took the children to the
H[…] Shelter in March 2009.  There were reports of her oversleeping and the
children not attending school while she was residing there.  In August 2009,
she was asked to leave the shelter.  On September 30, 2009, Maria apprehended
the children and placed them with T.G..

[
12
]

T.G. and her husband P.G. were approved by the
CAS as a "potential kinship placement" for the children.  They were
unable to make a commitment for the care of the children for the long term.  K.M.
and J.R. were not addressing their substance-abuse problems.  There was
conflict between them.  Their supervised access to the children had to be done
separately.  They put forth no plan for the long-term care of the children.  K.M.
gave the CAS a consent for them to receive information about her from the
methadone program.  J.R. refused to sign the consent.  Reports from the
methadone program indicated that K.M. had tested positive for cocaine and
opiates.  On April 26, 2010, the police executed a drug search warrant at the
residence of T.M..  J.R. and K.M. had been residing there, contrary to the
restraining order that they have no contact with each other.  When the police
attended they had left.  The police found a “grow op” for marijuana at the
residence.  T.M. was arrested and held in custody.  On April 27, J.R. and K.M.
turned themselves into the police.  They were charged with producing marijuana
and possession of marijuana for the purpose of trafficking.  Both were released
on bail.  J.R. was released on bail on a term that he resides with his mother
in Bracebridge, who was his surety.  Maria stated the following:

...

23)  To date K.M. and J.R. have not followed through with any of the
current expectations regarding their longstanding issues of family violence and
substance abuse.

24)  K.M. and J.R. are in no position to put forth a reliable plan
of care.  Furthermore, their record of breaches, substance abuse and complete
lack of follow through indicate that no plan can be expected to be forth
coming.

25)  The children are of the age where permanency is a priority and
as such, the Society respectfully requests that all the children be made Crown
Wards without access.

[
13
]

On Wednesday, June 2 when the matter came before
Justice McSorley, K.M. was not present, when she heard Mr. Lang's motion to be
removed from the record as her solicitor.  She came late and she was present
when the motion of the CAS for summary judgment was heard.  J.R. was not
present.  The following dialogue took place:

...

But
realistically, I’ve read the material, there’s been two-thirds of a year gone
by when three little people have been waiting for their parents to get their
act together and it’s not fair to them for me to make them wait while you do
that and to hope that you’ll do that because then if you don’t succeed, it’s
just a longer period of time.  And I suspect that’s very hard for you to hear
and I suspect you love all three of these kids very, very much but the fact is
that I have to be concerned about them first and I have to make decisions that
are in their best interests.

K.M.:   Yes, I
know.

[
14
]

Justice McSorley made the following endorsement:

June 2, 2010

Ms Torrance –
CAS

Mr Lang for
mother

The mother has
not been in touch with Mr Lang for several months despite his efforts to
contact her.  She did attend at his office yesterday and was served with the
motion.  She was advised to be in court by 9.30 a.m. this morning.  She is not
present – the waiting room was checked at 10.20 a.m.  Under the circumstances,
it is evident that her involvement in this matter is minimal and that she is
not communicating with her lawyer.

Order:

1.

Leave granted to Mr Lang to file his Notice of Motion and Affidavit
of Service on or before June 4/10 by 4.30 p.m.

2.

Mr Lang is removed as solicitor of record for the mother.

Motion for
Summary Judgment – mother present.

The parents
have put forward no viable plan for the immediate care of the children.  The
mother is entered Detox today and then intends to attend an in-care addictions
program.  Although it is hoped that the mother succeeds in maintaining sobriety
she is not in that position at this time.  The parents have been provided with
opportunities to access services since the children have been in care and they
have been either unwilling or unable to do so.  While I accept that the mother
has a heart-felt intention to turn her life around, the court must consider her
situation today and not rely on some future possibility.  There is no genuine
issue for trial.

3.

Final order to issue in terms of paragraphs 1-7 of the motion at Tab
11 of the Continuing Record.

4.

The trial dates of June 7-11 are vacated.

McSorley J.

Relevant Family Law Rules

[
15
]

RULE
1

FAILURE TO
FOLLOW RULES OR OBEY ORDER

1 (8) The court may
deal with a failure to follow these rules, or a failure to obey an order in the
case or a related case, by making any order that it considers necessary for a
just determination of the matter, on any conditions that the court considers
appropriate, including

RULE
2

PRIMARY
OBJECTIVE

2 (2) The primary objective of these rules is to enable the court
to deal with cases justly.

DEALING WITH
CASES JUSTLY

(3) Dealing with a
case justly includes,

(a) ensuring that the
procedure is fair to all parties;

(b) saving expense and
time;

(c) dealing with the
case in ways that are appropriate to its importance and complexity; and

(d) giving appropriate court resources to the case while taking
account of the need to give resources to other cases.

DUTY TO
PROMOTE PRIMARY OBJECTIVE

(4) The court is
required to apply these rules to promote the primary objective, and parties and
their lawyers are required to help the court to promote the primary objective.

RULE
3

COUNTING DAYS

3.(1) In these rules or an order, the number of days between two
events is counted as follows:

1. The first day is the day after the first event.

2. The last day is the day of the second event.

COUNTING DAYS -- SHORT
PERIODS

(2) If a rule or order provides a period of less than seven days
for something to be done, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court
offices are closed do not count as part of the period.

DAY WHEN
COURT OFFICES CLOSED

(3) If the last day of
a period of time under these rules or an order falls on a day when court
offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open.

(4) The following are
examples of how time is counted under these rules:

1. Notice of a motion
must be served not later than four days before the motion date (see subrule
14(11)). Saturday and Sunday are not counted, because the notice period is less
than seven days (see subrule (2)). Service on the day set out in the left
column below is in time for the motion to be heard on the day set out in the
right column below.

Service on             Motion may be heard on the following

Monday                               Friday

Tuesday                               Monday

Wednesday                          Tuesday

Thursday                              Wednesday

Friday                                  Thursday

Saturday                              Friday

Sunday                                Friday

RULE
6

EFFECTIVE
DATE, SERVICE BY COURIER

(10) Service of a document by courier is effective on the day
after the courier picks it up.

RULE
11

AMENDING ANSWER WITHOUT
COURT'S PERMISSION

(2) A respondent may amend the answer without the court's
permission as follows:

1. If the application has been amended, by serving and
filing an amended answer within 14 days after being served with the amended
application.

2.
If the application has not been amended, by serving and filing an amended
answer and also filing the consent of all parties to the amendment.

CHILD
PROTECTION, AMENDMENTS WITHOUT COURT'S PERMISSION

(2.1) In a child
protection case, if a significant change relating to the child happens after
the original document is filed,

(a) the applicant may serve and file an amended
application, an amended plan of care or both; and

(b) the respondent may serve and file an amended answer
and plan of care.

MOTION WITH
NOTICE

(11) A party making a
motion with notice shall,

(a) serve the
documents mentioned in subrule (9) or (10) on all other parties, not later than
four days before the motion date;

RULE 14 -- MOTIONS FOR
TEMPORARY ORDERS

DOCUMENTS
FOR A MOTION

(9) A motion, whether
made with or without notice,

(a) requires a notice
of motion (Form 14) and an affidavit (Form 14A); and

(b) may be supported by additional evidence.

PROCEDURAL,
UNCOMPLICATED OR UNOPPOSED MATTERS -- MOTION FORM

(10) If a motion is limited to procedural, uncomplicated or
unopposed matters, the party making the motion may use a motion form (Form 14B)
instead of a notice of motion and affidavit.

MOTION WITH NOTICE

(11) A party making a motion with notice shall,

(a) serve the
documents mentioned in subrule (9) or (10) on all other parties, not later than
four days before the motion date;

(b) file the documents
as soon as possible after service, but not later than two days before the
motion date; and

(c) file a
confirmation (Form 14C) not later than 2 p.m. two days before the motion date.

RULE
16

WHEN AVAILABLE

16.(1) After the respondent has served an answer or after the time
for serving an answer has expired, a party may make a motion for summary
judgment for a final order without a trial on all or part of any claim made or
any defence presented in the case.

AVAILABLE IN ANY CASE
EXCEPT DIVORCE

(2) A motion for summary judgment under subrule (1) may be made in
any case (including a child protection case) that does not include a divorce
claim.

EVIDENCE OF RESPONDING
PARTY

(4.1) In response to the affidavit or other evidence served by the
party making the motion, the party responding to the motion may not rest on
mere allegations or denials but shall set out, in an affidavit or other
evidence, specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue for trial.

EVIDENCE NOT FROM
PERSONAL KNOWLEDGE

(5) If a party's evidence is not from a person who has personal
knowledge of the facts in dispute, the court may draw conclusions unfavourable
to the party.

NO ISSUE FOR TRIAL

(6) If there is no genuine issue
requiring a trial of a claim or defence, the court shall make a final order
accordingly.

Analysis

[
16
]

J.R. was actually served with the summary
judgment motion and Maria's affidavit on Friday, May 28, 2010.  According to
Rule 14(11), the motion could not be heard until Thursday, June 3, 2010.  This
rule applies to a temporary order.  What was sought was a final order.  The CAS
amended its protection application to seek Crown Wardship without access on
Thursday, May 28, 2010.  J.R. was served with this document on Tuesday, June 1,
2010.  He was entitled to 14 days pursuant to Rule 11(2)1 to deliver an
answer.  Clearly the order granted by Justice McSorley on Wednesday, June 2,
2010 of Crown Wardship without access violated the rules with respect to time
and service.

[
17
]

I set out the test for summary judgment in child
protection proceedings and the standard of appellate review from a judgment for
summary judgment in
Children's Aid Society of the Regional Municipality of
Waterloo v. V.L.
2006 CanLII 32610 (ON SC)
, [2006] O.J.  No. 3785 (affirmed
2007 ONCA 113 (CanLII)
, 2007 O.J. No. 613 (Court
of Appeal)).

I stated the following:

48
The
Child
and Family Services Act
sets out principles defining the power of the state
through Children's Aid Societies to intervene in families to protect children.
Pursuant to sections 40 and 41 of the
Act
, a Society may bring an
application before the court for a hearing to determine whether a child is in
need of protection as defined by s. 37(2) of the
Act
and, assuming a
finding is made, for a disposition pursuant to s. 57. Rule 16 of the
Family
Law Rules
permits the court on application by the CAS on the basis of
affidavit evidence to make a summary judgment where there was no genuine issue
for trial. The CAS must disclose its full case to the court. The court must
take a "good, hard look" at the "full evidentiary record"
to determine if there are any factual issues in dispute which create a genuine
issue for trial (decision of Justice Hardman in
Children's Aid Society of
the Regional Municipality of Waterloo v. R.S.
,
2000 CanLII 22902 (ON CJ)
, [2000] O.J. No. 4880, paras.
22-23
). The respondent is
required to put her "best foot forward" in disclosing her case in
response to the case for the Society (decision of Justice Katarynych in
Children's
Aid Society of Toronto v. R.H
.,
2000 CanLII 3158 (ON CJ)
, [2000] O.J. No. 5853, para.
8
). The respondent cannot
"rest on mere allegations or denials". The respondent must set out in
affidavits "specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue for
trial" (Rule 16(4.1)). The CAS need not meet the test of "clearest of
cases" as in a motion for summary judgment under Rule 20 of the
Rules
of Civil Procedure
(decision of Justice Lane in
R.A.V. Jewish Family and
Child Service
,
[2001] O.J. No. 47 at para. 20
). The question of whether
there is a genuine issue for trial must be determined in the context of the
overarching principles set out in s. 1 of the
Act
that its primary
purpose is to "promote the best interests, protection and well being of
children". This must be done considering the narrow time lines
constraining the available dispositions imposed on the court by sections 57 and
70 of the
Act
. Rule 16 provides a remedy "to contain and control a
child's drift in litigation" (para. 14 of
R.H.
, supra). It is meant
to prevent a child being held in "limbo" while a dysfunctional parent
engages in uncertain attempts to correct his or her inadequacies (
R.H.
,
supra, para.
16
).

I held that the standard of appellate was somewhere between
"palpable and overriding error" and correctness.

[
18
]

Counsel for J.R. emphasized the concern that
courts have expressed that parents in child protection cases be granted
procedural fairness.  She referred to the cases of
Children's Aid Society of
Halton Region v. C.J.R
2005 ONCJ 514 (CanLII)
, [2005] O.J. No. 5786 at paras.
20
, 27 and 29,
Children
and Family Services for York Region v. E.T.
2009 CanLII 72329 (ON SC)
, [2009] O.J. No. 5587 at paras.

18
, 25 and 35 and
A.M. v. Chatham-Kent Integrated Children's Service
Children's Aid Society

[2006] O.J. No. 2984 at paras. 53
, 65 and 68.

[
19
]

Counsel for the CAS emphasized the importance of
the best interest of the children in trial protection proceedings.  She referred
to the decision of the Court of Appeal in
The Children's Aid Society of
Toronto v. D.P. and R.L.
2005 CanLII 34560 (ON CA)
, [2005] O.J. No, 4075. In this case the Court of
Appeal held that the Superior Court Appeal Judge erred when she remitted the
case to the trial court to determine whether or not the mother should have
access to children who had been made crown wards.  The court stated the
following:

9
It is
clear from the CFSA and from the jurisprudence that the overriding concern for
the best interests of the child can only be satisfied if proceedings are
conducted in a timely fashion and delay is avoided. The CAS cannot place a
Crown Ward for adoption if an access order is outstanding: CFSA, s. 140(2). In
view of the concurrent findings of the trial judge and the appeal judge that Crown
Wardship was justified, and that the best interests of the child would be met
through the CAS plan for adoption, it is imperative that these children not be
left in what counsel for the Office of the Children's Lawyer aptly described as
"litigation limbo". As this court stated in Children's Aid Society of
Peel v. W.(M.J.)
(1995),
1995 CanLII 593 (ON CA)
,
23
O.R. (3d) 174
at 200, "Time is important in the life of a young
child." These children have been the subject of CAS concern from the time
of their birth. More than two years have passed since the CAS commenced
proceedings to have them made Crown Wards so that they could be placed for
adoption. Remitting the matter for yet another hearing, especially as the fresh
evidence does not satisfy us that the mother has any hope of satisfying the
onus under s. 59(2)(b), would be contrary to the best interests of these
children and to the policy of the CSFA.

[
20
]

She also referred to the decision of the Supreme
Court of Canada in the judgment of Justice L’Heureux Dube in
Children's Aid
Society of Toronto v. C.M.
1994 CanLII 83 (SCC)
, [1994] 2 S.C.R. 165 as follows:

41
Finally, it is clear
that the best interests of a child require different solutions over time and
such interests may have to take precedence over any parental interests. As was
recently said in Young v. Young, supra, at p. 60, the "furtherance and
protection of the child's best interests must take priority over the desires
and interests of the parent". Further, as examined in New Brunswick
(Minister of Health and Community Services) v. S.G. and S.A.
(1989),
1989 CanLII 160 (NB CA)
,
100 N.B.R. (2d) 357
, at p. 360,
a child's best
interests must take precedence over all other considerations including the
effect of delay:

While it is correct to say there
were administrative delays in the processing of the guardianship application in
this case, there is no proof that the delays were deliberate or that there was
any bad faith on the part of anyone involved in the proceedings. Moreover it is
to be observed that the trial judge never lost sight of the fact that the sole
issue before him was to determine what was in the "best interest" of
the child S.G. Jr.

[
21
]

The evidence is of a failed relationship between
K.M. and J.R..  There is no evidence that J.R. has ever provided care for the
children alone and that he would ever be able to do so in the future.  There is
no evidence of an employment record of J.R..  The evidence is of violence and
marital conflict between him and K.M..  The evidence is that J.R. was addicted
to both prescription and non-prescription drugs and that he failed to seek
treatment for his addiction.

[
22
]

I do not condone the rush to judgment by the
CAS.  A better approach would have been for the CAS to ask Justice McSorley for
an adjournment for three weeks to permit J.R. to file material if he wished to
do so.  However, J.R. has not demonstrated that he has a viable plan for the
care of the children.  To send the matter back to Provincial Court now to
permit him to attempt to do so would, in my view, delay the inevitable outcome,
which is what Justice McSorley ordered.  I find what Justice Katarynych said in

Children's Aid Society of Toronto v. R.H.

2000 CanLII 3158 (ON CJ)
, [2000] O.J. No. 5853 to be
particularly applicable to this case:

16
Child
development does not wait. Multiple issues of parental dysfunction cannot be
quickly changed. The child is not to be held in limbo waiting for change in a
parent that is unlikely to happen. The parent's chance to correct parenting
inadequacies must be balanced with a child's right to appropriate development
within a realistic time frame, if damage to the child is to be minimized. See
Children's Aid Society of Kingston and Frontenac County v. J.G. and D.B.
(1997),
1997 CanLII 17031 (ON CTGD)
,
73 A.C.W.S. (3d) 82
,
[1997] O.J. No. 3205
,
1997 CarswellOnt 2830 (Ont. Fam.
Ct.)
, per Justice Cheryl J. Robertson.

17
The
court's function is very narrow in this motion. The task is not to resolve an
issue of fact but to determine whether a genuine issue of fact exists. The
issue must be germane to the judicial decision required in the case. A
"genuine" issue of fact requires that the fact be material to the
decision that must be taken in the main litigation. If the result of the
proceeding does not turn on the existence or non-existence of the fact that is
advanced as a genuine issue, then it cannot relate to a "genuine issue for
trial". See Irving Ungerman Ltd. v. Galanis
(1991),
1991 CanLII 7275 (ON CA)
,
4 O.R. (3d) 545
,
50 O.A.C. 176
,
83 D.L.R. (4th) 734
,
1 C.P.C. (3d) 248
,
[1991] O.J. No. 1478
,
1991 CarswellOnt 370 (Ont. C.A.)
, at
pages 550-552 [O.R.]
.

18
In
child protection proceedings, the genuineness of an issue must arise from
something more than a heartfelt expression of a parent's desire to resume care
of the child. There must be an arguable notion discernible from the parent's
evidence that she faces some better prospects than what existed at the time of
the society's removal of the child from her care and has developed some new
ability as a parent. See Children's Aid Society of London and Middlesex v. L.A.
and H.C. (No. 1),
1999 CanLII 20470 (ON CTGD)
,
[1999] O.J. No. 5839
,
1999 CarswellOnt 4679 (Ont. Fam.
Ct.)
, per Justice Henry Vogelsang.

Conclusion

[
23
]

Justice McSorley's decision satisfies the test
for summary judgment on the material before her.  There is no relevant fresh evidence.
J.R.'s statements in his affidavit sworn September 24, 2010 of future
intentions are general statements in boilerplate language without particulars.
The appeal is dismissed.
